title: Der alte Großvater und der Enkel
titleEn: The Old Grandfather and the Grandson
part: The Old Grandfather and the Grandson
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 78. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (mußte, floß, fiengen, alsofort).
about: KHM 78, and barely a page long — a household parable rather than a fairy tale, with no magic in it at all. An old man whose hands shake is banished from the table to a corner behind the stove, until his four-year-old grandson, fitting little boards together on the floor, explains what he is making. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as mußte, floß, fiengen and alsofort.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein steinalter Mann, dem waren die Augen trüb geworden, die Ohren taub, und die Knie zitterten ihm.
sentences.l: There was once a stone-old man, to whom the eyes had grown dim, the ears deaf, and the knees trembled on him.
sentences.i: There was once a man as old as the hills, whose eyes had grown dim and his ears deaf, and whose knees trembled under him.
sentences.n: steinalt — literally “stone-old,” for ancient. dem… and ihm are the familiar dative of possession: “his eyes,” “his knees.”

sentences.t: Wenn er nun bei Tische saß und den Löffel kaum halten konnte, schüttete er Suppe auf das Tischtuch, und es floß ihm auch etwas wieder aus dem Mund.
sentences.l: When he now sat at table and could scarcely hold the spoon, he poured soup onto the tablecloth, and something also ran out of his mouth again.
sentences.i: When he sat at table and could scarcely hold his spoon, he spilled soup on the cloth, and some of it would run back out of his mouth.
sentences.n: bei Tische — an old dative in -e, kept alive in fixed phrases; “at table.”

sentences.t: Sein Sohn und dessen Frau ekelten sich davor, und deswegen mußte sich der alte Großvater endlich hinter den Ofen in die Ecke setzen, und sie gaben ihm sein Essen in ein irdenes Schüsselchen und noch dazu nicht einmal satt;
sentences.l: His son and the latter’s wife were disgusted at it, and therefore the old grandfather had at last to sit himself behind the stove in the corner, and they gave him his food in an earthen little-bowl, and moreover not even his fill;
sentences.i: His son and the son’s wife were disgusted by it, and so the old grandfather had at last to sit in the corner behind the stove; and they gave him his food in a little earthenware bowl, and not even enough of it at that;
sentences.n: dessen is the genitive of der used as a possessive — “his,” meaning the son’s, where a plain sein could have meant the grandfather’s. “nicht einmal satt” leaves out the noun: not even [enough to eat his] fill.

sentences.t: da sah er betrübt nach dem Tisch, und die Augen wurden ihm naß.
sentences.l: then he looked sorrowfully toward the table, and the eyes grew wet on him.
sentences.i: and he would look sadly across at the table, and his eyes would grow wet.
sentences.n: da at the head of a clause is “then, and so,” not “there.” “die Augen wurden ihm naß” — the dative of possession again.

sentences.t: Einmal auch konnten seine zitterigen Hände das Schüsselchen nicht fest halten, es fiel zur Erde und zerbrach.
sentences.l: Once too his trembling hands could not hold the little-bowl fast, it fell to the earth and broke.
sentences.i: One time, too, his shaking hands could not hold the little bowl firmly; it fell to the ground and broke.
sentences.n: zitterig (modern zittrig) is formed straight off zittern, to tremble. “zur Erde” here is the floor, not the planet.

sentences.t: Die junge Frau schalt, er sagte aber nichts und seufzte nur.
sentences.l: The young wife scolded, but he said nothing and only sighed.
sentences.n: schalt is the past of schelten, to scold, a strong verb nearly gone from ordinary modern use. The “junge Frau” is the son’s wife — young set against the old man.

sentences.t: Da kaufte sie ihm ein hölzernes Schüsselchen für ein paar Heller, daraus mußte er nun essen.
sentences.l: Then she bought him a wooden little-bowl for a couple of Heller, out of which he now had to eat.
sentences.i: Then she bought him a little wooden bowl for a few Heller, and out of that he had to eat from then on.
sentences.n: A Heller was the smallest copper coin there was; “ein paar Heller” is pennies. Wood is what you buy for someone whose bowls you expect to be broken.

sentences.t: Wie sie da so sitzen, so trägt der kleine Enkel von vier Jahren auf der Erde kleine Brettlein zusammen.
sentences.l: As they are sitting there like that, the little grandson of four years is carrying little boards together on the ground.
sentences.i: As they were sitting there, the little grandson, four years old, was gathering small boards together on the floor.
sentences.n: The tale slips into the present tense (sitzen, trägt) for exactly the sentence that turns it, and drops back into the past immediately after — a storyteller’s move. The literal keeps the present; ordinary English narrative will not carry it.

sentences.t: „Was machst du da?“ fragte der Vater.
sentences.l: “What are you making there?” asked the father.

sentences.t: „Ich mache ein Tröglein,“ antwortete das Kind, „daraus sollen Vater und Mutter essen, wenn ich groß bin.“
sentences.l: “I am making a little-trough,” answered the child, “out of it father and mother shall eat, when I am big.”
sentences.i: “I am making a little trough,” answered the child; “father and mother are to eat out of it when I am grown.”
sentences.n: A Trog is the wooden trough that animals are fed from, and the diminutive does not soften it. The child is not being cruel — he is simply arranging the future as he has seen it arranged.

sentences.t: Da sahen sich Mann und Frau eine Weile an, fiengen endlich an zu weinen, holten alsofort den alten Großvater an den Tisch und ließen ihn von nun an immer mit essen, sagten auch nichts wenn er ein wenig verschüttete.
sentences.l: Then man and wife looked at each other a while, began at last to weep, fetched the old grandfather forthwith to the table and let him from now on always eat along, said nothing either when he spilled a little.
sentences.i: Then husband and wife looked at one another a while, and at last began to weep; they brought the old grandfather to the table at once and let him always eat with them from then on, and said nothing when he spilled a little.
sentences.n: alsofort is an older sofort, “at once.”
